red.summary: Learn what separates a law from a gunman's order. Meet the three classic answers to why law binds, so every later lesson has a frame to hang on.

sections.title: The Gunman and the Tax Bill
sections.body_md: A robber says "your money or your life." The tax office also demands your money and can punish you if you refuse. Both are orders backed by threats, yet we call only one of them law. Jurisprudence, the study of what law is, starts here: what makes a demand law, and why should anyone obey it? Lawyers need the answer, because a client's home, savings or freedom often turns on whether a rule truly binds.

sections.title: Three Classic Answers
sections.body_md: Natural law theory says law must serve reason and the common good. Thomas Aquinas defined law as an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by whoever cares for the community, and made public. Legal positivism says law is a social fact: John Austin, writing in 1832, called it the command of a sovereign, backed by a sanction, where the sovereign is whoever the people habitually obey. Legal realism, led by Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., says law is what courts will actually do.
sections.example: Ask whether a city's curfew is law. The natural lawyer asks whether it serves the common good. The positivist asks whether the right body enacted it. The realist asks whether the police and courts will enforce it.

sections.title: Obliged Versus Having an Obligation
sections.body_md: H.L.A. Hart, in The Concept of Law (1961), said Austin's theory makes the state a gunman writ large. The gunman leaves you obliged, meaning forced by fear. Law claims more. It claims you have an obligation, a reason to comply even when no one is watching. That claim is what this course calls authority: the right to tell you what to do, not only the power to make you do it.
sections.example: At 3 a.m., on an empty road with no cameras, a driver stops at a red light. Fear of a ticket cannot explain it. She stops because she treats the rule as a reason. That is the difference Hart saw.

yellow.summary: You know the authority question and the three classic answers. Now learn how Hart and Kelsen explain, step by step, where a legal system gets its authority.

sections.title: Hart's Union of Rules
sections.body_md: You learned that Hart rejected the gunman model. His replacement says a legal system joins two kinds of rules. Primary rules tell people what to do, such as do not steal. Secondary rules are rules about rules. Rules of change say how to make or repeal law. Rules of adjudication say who settles disputes. The rule of recognition says which rules count as law at all. Hart said secondary rules cure the defects of a simple society run on custom alone: uncertainty, rigidity and slow enforcement.
sections.example: A village that settles disputes only by custom cannot change a bad custom quickly or tell which custom applies. A legislature, courts and a rulebook for identifying law fix those three defects.

sections.title: Recognition and the Internal Point of View
sections.body_md: The rule of recognition is not written in any one statute. It exists because officials, especially judges, actually use it to identify law. Hart called this the internal point of view: officials treat the rule as a standard to guide and criticize conduct, not just a habit. They need not think it morally good. A judge may accept it out of duty, tradition or self-interest. Authority, for Hart, is a social practice among officials.

sections.title: Kelsen's Chain of Validity
sections.body_md: Hans Kelsen's Pure Theory of Law pictured law as a ladder. A parking ticket is valid because a regulation allows it, the regulation because a statute does, the statute because the constitution does. What makes the first constitution valid? Kelsen answered with the basic norm, or Grundnorm, a presupposition that the historically first constitution ought to be obeyed. It is assumed, not enacted, so the chain can end. Kelsen added that a legal order must be by and large effective to be valid.
sections.example: A ticket for parking in a bus lane traces up: the ticket rests on a city rule, the city rule on a state statute, the statute on the state constitution, and that constitution on the presupposed basic norm.

orange.summary: You know how Hart and Kelsen ground authority in social facts. Now see where those accounts break: Raz's sharper theory, Dworkin's attack, and courts that used Kelsen to bless coups.

sections.title: Raz's Service Conception
sections.body_md: Hart explained when people accept a rule, but not when authority is deserved. Joseph Raz filled that gap. His normal justification thesis says an authority is legitimate when you would better follow the reasons that already apply to you by obeying it than by deciding alone. A good authority serves you, like a trusted pilot. Its directives are preemptive: they replace your own weighing rather than adding one more reason to the pile. Raz argued that law always claims this authority, even when it lacks it.
sections.example: A pharmacist tells you not to combine two drugs. You do not reweigh the chemistry yourself. You follow her because doing so better serves your own goal of staying healthy. Raz says legitimate law works the same way.

sections.title: Dworkin's Attack and the Positivist Split
sections.body_md: Ronald Dworkin argued that judges apply moral principles that no rule of recognition lists, so positivism misdescribes law. Positivists split. Inclusive positivists, such as Hart in his Postscript and Jules Coleman, say a rule of recognition may include moral tests if officials accept them. Exclusive positivists, following Raz's sources thesis, say law's content must be identifiable from social facts alone. Otherwise law could not guide people who disagree about morality, which is its main job.

sections.title: When Success Becomes Legality
sections.body_md: Kelsen's efficacy test became courtroom doctrine. In State v. Dosso (1958), Pakistan's Supreme Court relied on Kelsen to hold that a successful coup creates a new legal order. Other courts facing coups reasoned similarly. The lesson is stark: a theory that ties validity to effective power can turn a general's success into law. This is where a purely descriptive account of authority stops protecting the people law is meant to serve.

sections.title: Law and Violence
sections.body_md: Robert Cover, in Violence and the Word (1986), reminded theorists that legal interpretation takes place in a field of pain and death. A judge's reading of a statute can send a person to prison, and others carry out that violence because they obey the judge. In Nomos and Narrative (1983), Cover argued that communities create their own legal meanings, and that state courts are jurispathic: by choosing one meaning, they kill off rivals. Authority, on this view, is never only an idea. It is the power to turn a reading of words into force against a body.
sections.example: Picture a client jailed under a decree issued the morning after a coup. If efficacy alone makes law, her lawyer has nothing to argue. A theory of authority decides whether she has a case.

sections.title: Law as a Plan
sections.body_md: Scott Shapiro's Legality (2011) argues that law is a social plan for a community too large or divided to plan informally. Plans guide without needing moral agreement, which explains how law binds people who disagree. Shapiro also faces the bootstrapping puzzle Hart met: how can people without authority create rules that give them authority? His answer is that planning is a capacity we all have, and shared plans can authorize officials. Critics ask whether a plan's existence ever creates a genuine duty.
sections.example: Housemates make a chore chart. No one is a king, yet the chart settles who takes out the trash, even for the housemate who thinks the split is unfair. Shapiro says a legal system is that chart at the scale of a nation.

sections.title: The Natural Law Reply
sections.body_md: John Finnis, in Natural Law and Natural Rights (1980), revived Aquinas for modern readers. He argued that authority is justified because communities need coordination to secure basic goods such as life, knowledge and friendship. Law in its central case is just law. An unjust law is law in a watered-down sense: it may be valid as a social fact, yet it lacks full moral authority. Finnis offers what Dosso lacked: a reason to deny a general's decree full authority.
sections.example: A valid statute orders landlords to evict tenants of a disfavored religion. Finnis would say it is law in a technical sense, yet it fails law's purpose, so its claim on conscience collapses.

sections.title: Religious Accounts of Authority
sections.body_md: Religious legal traditions face the same puzzle in another form. Jewish law draws authority from the covenant at Sinai, yet a famous Talmudic story, the oven of Akhnai, has the rabbis outvote a heavenly voice, declaring that the Torah is not in heaven: once given, its meaning belongs to human interpreters. Maimonides' Mishneh Torah, a twelfth century code, organized that law for ordinary readers. Islamic jurisprudence grounds law in divine command read through the method of usul al-fiqh, which PSU-5.2 develops. Each tradition must answer who may say what a binding text means.

sections.title: Building Your Position
sections.body_md: Your mastery task asks you to decide a case where a valid rule demands an unjust result. Start by choosing what authority should rest on: acceptance, service, planning or the common good. Then test it on the hardest case for your view. A positivist must explain why legal validity still matters when a rule is evil. A natural lawyer must explain who decides what is just. A strong answer names its cost openly. red.summary: Learn what a legal right is and who it binds. Rights are the main tools lawyers use to protect people, so this idea returns in every course.

sections.title: A Right Is a Claim Others Must Respect
sections.body_md: A right is a claim, backed by law, that someone else must respect. A wish is something you hope for. A right is something others owe you. When a right is ignored, the holder can ask a court to act. Rights let ordinary people stand up to the powerful, and lawyers turn them into protection for clients' homes, work and freedom.
sections.example: Maria's lease says her landlord may not enter without 24 hours' notice. One morning he walks in unannounced. Maria does not merely wish for privacy. She holds a right, and the landlord broke a duty.

sections.title: Rights Against People and Against the State
sections.body_md: Some rights bind private persons, such as a buyer's right to the goods she paid for. Others bind the state, such as the right not to be jailed without a fair trial. Every right points at someone with a matching duty. If no one holds a duty, the right is empty. This pairing, a right on one side and a duty on the other, is the basic shape lawyers look for in every problem.
sections.example: A shop refuses to hand over a sofa a customer paid for. Her right runs against the shop. Police hold a protester for a week with no hearing. His right runs against the state. Same word, different duty holders.

sections.title: Legal Rights and Moral Rights
sections.body_md: A legal right exists because a legal system recognizes it. A moral right exists, if it does, because of morality, whether or not any law agrees. John Locke argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property before any government. Jeremy Bentham, a founder of positivism, mocked natural rights as "nonsense upon stilts" and said only law creates rights. The gap between the two matters most when a law denies what people believe they are owed.

sections.title: Four Meanings of One Word
sections.body_md: You learned that a right pairs with a duty. Wesley Newcomb Hohfeld, in work published in 1913 and 1917, showed that is only one kind of right. A claim right means someone owes you a duty. A privilege, or liberty, means you owe no duty not to act. A power means you can change legal relations, such as making a will. An immunity means someone else cannot change your legal position. Lawyers who blur these four make arguments that sound strong and fail.

sections.title: Correlatives
sections.body_md: Each Hohfeld advantage has a correlative, a matching position held by the other person. Claim pairs with duty. Privilege pairs with no-right, meaning the other person cannot demand that you stop. Power pairs with liability, meaning exposure to having your position changed. Immunity pairs with disability, meaning lack of power to change someone's position. Reading a dispute as pairs of positions shows exactly who can demand what from whom.
sections.example: Your neighbor has a privilege to paint her fence purple. You hold a no-right: you cannot demand she stop, however much you dislike it. If she promised in writing not to, she would owe a duty and you would hold a claim.

sections.title: Using the Map on a Client Problem
sections.body_md: Hohfeld's map turns a vague complaint into precise questions. A client who says "I have a right" may mean she can demand action, may act freely, may change a legal arrangement, or is shielded from someone else's change. Each meaning calls for different proof and remedies. Asking which one she holds is often the first step to winning her case.
sections.example: You own a garden. You have a privilege to walk in it, a claim that strangers keep out, a power to sell it, and an immunity against a neighbor giving it away. Four rights, four different arguments.

orange.summary: You know Hohfeld's map of what rights are. Now see where the theories of why someone holds a right break down, through the will theory, the interest theory and the cases that defeat each.

sections.title: The Will Theory
sections.body_md: Hohfeld mapped rights but did not say what makes someone a right holder. The will theory, defended by Hart, says a right gives its holder control over another's duty. You hold the right if you can waive, enforce or release it. This fits contracts well: a creditor may forgive a debt. It breaks on infants, who cannot exercise control, and on rights the law makes unwaivable, such as the right not to be enslaved. On the will theory, these seem not to be rights.
sections.example: A lender forgives a friend's loan with a single text message. The power to release the debt is exactly what the will theory says makes the lender a right holder.

sections.title: The Interest Theory
sections.body_md: The interest theory, defended by Raz and Neil MacCormick, says you hold a right when an aspect of your well-being is a sufficient reason to hold someone else under a duty. This explains children's rights and unwaivable rights easily. It breaks on overbreadth: many people benefit from duties without holding rights. If you promise a friend to repay a loan, the friend's family benefits when you pay, yet only the friend holds the right.
sections.example: A daycare center contracts with a parent to supervise her son. The boy is the one protected, yet the parent signed. The interest theory says the boy holds a right. The will theory says only the parent does.

sections.title: Trumps and Side Constraints
sections.body_md: You know rights protect interests or choices. How strong should they be? Dworkin, in Taking Rights Seriously (1977), said rights are trumps over collective goals: the state may not override them just because doing so raises overall welfare. Robert Nozick, in Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), called rights side constraints, limits on how anyone may pursue goals at all. Both resist pure counting of costs and benefits. The open question is what happens when honoring a right risks catastrophe.
sections.example: A city could reduce crime by searching every home at random. The total benefit might be large. Rights as trumps say the city may not do it, however good the numbers look.

sections.title: When Rights Collide

sections.example: A hiker caught in a blizzard breaks into an empty cabin and burns the owner's firewood to survive. Most agree he acted rightly. Most also agree he owes the owner for the wood. That is a justified infringement.

red.summary: Learn what a legal duty is and how it differs from a moral duty. Most legal disputes begin with the question of whether a duty existed and was broken.

sections.title: What a Duty Is
sections.body_md: A duty is something the law requires you to do or not do. Drivers must stop at red lights. Employers must pay wages. A duty is the other side of a right: if Sam has a right to be paid, his employer has a duty to pay him. When a duty is broken, the person harmed can ask the law for help, and a lawyer's first job is often to prove the duty existed.
sections.example: A delivery company promises to drop off a wheelchair by Friday. It now has a duty to the buyer. If it fails and the buyer misses a medical appointment, the broken duty is the start of her claim.

sections.title: Legal and Moral Duties
sections.body_md: Some duties are moral but not legal. Most places do not legally require you to thank a friend or keep a lunch date. Some duties are legal but morally neutral, such as filing a form by a deadline. Many overlap: do not steal, do not hit. Jurisprudence asks how these two kinds of duty relate, and whether a legal duty that is morally wrong still truly binds.
sections.example: You promise to help a friend move on Saturday and then skip it. Your friend is rightly upset, yet no court will hear the case. You broke a moral duty, not a legal one.

sections.title: Duty as Liability to Punishment
sections.body_md: You learned that a duty is what law requires. But what makes it a requirement? Austin said you have a legal duty when you are liable to a sanction if you disobey a command. Kelsen refined this: a duty exists when the law attaches a sanction to the opposite conduct. On both views, the threat defines the duty. That leaves a gap, because many rules carry no punishment, such as the rules for making a valid will.
sections.example: A sign says No Parking, Fine 50 Dollars. On Austin's view, your duty not to park is simply your exposure to that fine. Remove the fine and, for Austin, the duty disappears.

That leaves a gap, because many rules carry no punishment, such as the rules for making a valid will. Example: A sign says No Parking, Fine 50 Dollars. On Austin's view, your duty not to park is simply your exposure to that fine. Remove the fine and, for Austin, the duty disappears.

sections.title: Hart's Correction
sections.body_md: Hart said duties arise from rules backed by serious social pressure and accepted as standards, not from the odds of punishment. He also showed that power-conferring rules, such as rules for wills, marriages and contracts, give people facilities rather than duties. If you skip the required witness, you are not punished. Your will simply fails. Calling that failure a sanction twists ordinary understanding. Law does more than forbid: it helps people arrange their lives.

sections.title: Holmes and the Bad Man

For that person, a duty is simply a prediction that a court will impose a cost if he acts. Holmes did not praise the bad man. He used him to strip moral words away so lawyers could see what the law actually does. This is a founding idea of legal realism.
sections.example: A factory owner asks only one thing: if I dump waste in the river, what will a court make me pay? Holmes said that question, cold as it is, shows what the law actually requires of him.

orange.summary: You know the theories of what a legal duty is. Now see where they break on a harder question: is there any general moral duty to obey law just because it is law?

sections.title: Why Obey Because It Is Law?
sections.body_md: You learned how theorists define legal duty. Political obligation asks something else: a moral duty to obey law because it is law. Socrates, in Plato's Crito, refused to escape his death sentence, arguing he had agreed to the city's laws by living there. John Locke grounded obligation in consent. Hart, in a 1955 essay, proposed fair play: if you benefit from others' cooperation under rules, you owe your share. Rawls defended a natural duty to support just institutions.
sections.example: A town builds a water system paid for by everyone's fees. A resident who taps in without paying takes the benefit of others' sacrifice. Fair play says he owes his share, whether or not he ever consented.

John Simmons, in Moral Principles and Political Obligations (1979), found that few people ever consent and many benefits are not voluntarily accepted. Raz agreed there is no general duty but allowed an attitude of respect for law that people may choose. The consensus among philosophers now leans skeptical.

sections.title: Civil Disobedience
sections.body_md: You know many philosophers doubt a general duty to obey. Then when is breaking law right? Martin Luther King Jr.'s Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963) argued that an unjust law is out of harmony with moral law, and that one who breaks it must do so openly, lovingly and with willingness to accept the penalty. Rawls defined civil disobedience as a public, nonviolent, conscientious breach of law aimed at changing law or policy. Henry David Thoreau's earlier essay framed it as individual conscience.
sections.example: In 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, broke a segregation law openly, and accepted arrest. Her act fits every element of the classic definition.

sections.title: Philosophical Anarchism
sections.body_md: Robert Paul Wolff, in In Defense of Anarchism (1970), argued that personal autonomy, the duty to decide for yourself, can never be reconciled with a duty to obey authority. Few accept his conclusion that no state is legitimate, but his argument sharpens the question. If any duty to obey exists, it must be compatible with thinking for yourself. Raz's service conception is one attempt: you obey because it helps you act on your own best reasons.

A strong answer ties the role to its purpose: the adversary system protects people's lives and freedoms by ensuring everyone has a voice. PSU-9.1 develops professional ethics.
sections.example: A defense lawyer learns her client committed the theft charged. She may not reveal it, and she may still hold the state to its proof. The rule protects every accused person, including the innocent.

sections.title: Mill's Harm Principle
sections.body_md: John Stuart Mill, in On Liberty (1859), argued that the only purpose for which power can rightfully be used over anyone, against their will, is to prevent harm to others. A person's own good is not enough. On this view, the state may ban drunk driving, because it endangers others, but not a dangerous hobby that risks only the person who chooses it.
sections.example: Two neighbors: one rides a motorcycle without a helmet on a private track, the other races through a school zone. Mill would let the state stop only the second, because only he puts other people at risk.

sections.title: What Counts as Harm to Others
sections.body_md: Harm, in its plain sense, means damage to someone's body, property, money or freedom. It is not the same as dislike. Neighbors may hate your haircut, your religion or your politics, but their distaste is not harm in Mill's sense. Mill also protected thought, speech and ways of living, which he called experiments in living, because a free society learns from them.
sections.example: A town council wants to fine a resident for painting her house bright orange. Neighbors say it lowers their mood. Under Mill's test, the council must show real damage to others, not mere distaste.

sections.title: Why Lawyers Care
sections.body_md: Harm is the hinge of many legal questions. A criminal charge usually needs a harm or a risk to others. A lawsuit for damages needs an injury. When a client is accused, a careful lawyer asks who was harmed and how. If no one was, the law may be overreaching. The harm principle lets the lawyer defend a client's liberty against rules that only express disapproval.
sections.example: A client is charged with selling raw milk to adults who asked for it and signed a warning. His lawyer's first question is who was harmed. The answer shapes the whole defense.

sections.title: Devlin's Challenge
sections.body_md: You learned that Mill allows coercion only to prevent harm to others. In 1957 the Wolfenden Report in Britain applied that idea, recommending decriminalizing private homosexual conduct between consenting adults, because some private morality is not the law's business. Patrick Devlin, a senior judge, objected in his 1959 lecture The Enforcement of Morals. He argued that a society is held together by shared morality and may defend itself against conduct ordinary people find deeply offensive, just as it defends against treason.

sections.title: Hart's Reply
sections.body_md: Hart answered in Law, Liberty and Morality (1963). He said Devlin offered no evidence that private conduct destroys societies, and that a shared morality can change without collapse. Hart also warned that enforcing majority disgust punishes people for who they are rather than for harm they cause. Parliament largely followed Wolfenden in 1967, and later law across many countries moved in the same direction.
sections.example: Devlin's test was the reaction of the reasonable person on public transport. Hart replied that intense disgust in a crowd proves only that people are disgusted, not that anyone is harmed.

sections.title: Harm as a Wrongful Setback
sections.body_md: You know Hart and Devlin fought over enforcing morality, but neither defined harm precisely. Joel Feinberg did, in his four-volume The Moral Limits of the Criminal Law (1984 to 1988). Harm, he said, is a wrongful setback to someone's interests. Both parts matter. A business that loses customers to fair competition suffers a setback, but no wrong. Without this second part, the harm principle swells to cover anything someone dislikes.
sections.example: A new bakery opens and the old one loses half its customers. Its interests are set back, but no one wronged it. Compare a rival who burns the old bakery down: setback plus wrong, so harm.

sections.title: The Offense Principle
sections.body_md: Feinberg added an offense principle: law may sometimes prohibit serious offense to others, such as public indecency, even without harm. He limited it with balancing factors: how intense and widespread the offense is, how easily it can be avoided, and the value of the conduct. Speech and art weigh heavily on the side of liberty. A single principle rarely settles a case. The fight is over which interests count and how much.
sections.example: A billboard shows a graphic image on a highway every commuter must pass. A gallery shows the same image behind a door with a warning. The offense is equal, but only the gallery's viewers can easily avoid it.

sections.title: Consent

sections.title: The Collapse Thesis
sections.body_md: You know Feinberg tightened harm to wrongful setbacks. Bernard Harcourt argued in 1999 that the harm principle had collapsed anyway. Once moralists learned to describe almost any conduct as harmful, saying for example that drug use harms communities, the principle could no longer separate legitimate from illegitimate bans. Harm became a universal password. The lesson is that harm talk can hide contested moral judgments.
sections.example: Opponents of a public smoking ban once argued it was mere moralism. Supporters answered with secondhand smoke data. Both sides spoke the language of harm, which is Harcourt's point: harm talk alone did not settle it.

sections.title: Autonomy and Perfectionism
sections.body_md: Raz, in The Morality of Freedom (1986), rebuilt the harm principle around autonomy. The state may promote valuable options for living, but coercion itself harms autonomy, so it must be used only to prevent harm, including harm to the conditions that let people choose their own lives. This is perfectionist liberalism: the state is not neutral about the good life, yet it limits force. It explains why a state may fund libraries but not jail people for not reading.
sections.example: A state funds free art classes to widen people's options. That is permitted perfectionism. Jailing people for skipping the classes would harm their autonomy, so Raz would forbid it.

sections.title: The But-For Test
sections.body_md: Causation means one thing bringing about another. The law's first and simplest test is called the but-for test: would the harm have happened but for, meaning without, the defendant's act? If not, the act is a factual cause. If the harm would have happened anyway, the act did not cause it, and the defendant is usually not liable for it.
sections.example: A driver runs a red light and hits a cyclist. But for the driver running the light, the crash would not have happened, so his act is a factual cause. If a tree had fallen on the cyclist at the same moment anyway, the answer changes.

sections.title: Factual Cause and Legal Cause
sections.body_md: Many events are but-for causes. The cyclist's crash also required that she bought a bike and that the driver's parents met. Law cannot blame all of them. So it adds a second test, legal cause, often called proximate cause in U.S. law. It asks whether the link between act and harm is close enough to make the actor responsible. Factual cause asks what happened. Legal cause asks whom it is fair to blame.

sections.title: Why Causation Protects People
sections.body_md: Causation keeps the law honest. It stops the state, or a plaintiff, from blaming someone for a harm they did not bring about, however unpopular they are. It also protects victims, because a defendant who did cause harm cannot escape by pointing to background conditions. A lawyer who masters causation can defend the wrongly blamed and win for the truly injured.
sections.example: A man with a criminal record is near a burglary when it happens. Without proof that his acts caused the loss, being disliked and nearby is not enough. Causation protects him.

sections.title: Common Sense Causation
sections.body_md: You learned that legal cause separates blameworthy links from mere background. Hart and Tony Honoré, in Causation in the Law (1959), argued that courts use ordinary common sense ideas of cause. People pick out abnormal events, or deliberate human acts, as causes, and treat normal conditions as background. Oxygen is needed for a fire, but we blame the person who dropped a match. Law, they said, refines this everyday reasoning rather than inventing its own.
sections.example: A house burns down. Investigators do not name oxygen, though it was necessary. They name the space heater left on the bed, because it was the abnormal event.

sections.title: Breaking the Chain
sections.body_md: On Hart and Honoré's account, a free, deliberate and informed act by another person usually breaks the chain of causation. So does an abnormal coincidence. The first actor set the stage, but the second actor's choice becomes the cause in law. This is called a novus actus interveniens, a new intervening act. It reflects respect for human agency: each adult is answerable for their own free choices.
sections.example: A careless driver leaves his keys in a running car. A thief steals it and deliberately rams a rival's shop. The owner's carelessness is a but-for cause, but the thief's free choice is the legal cause.

sections.title: Foreseeability and Palsgraf
sections.body_md: In Palsgraf v. Long Island Railroad (1928), railroad guards pushed a man boarding a train. He dropped a package of fireworks, which exploded, and something fell on Helen Palsgraf far down the platform. Judge Benjamin Cardozo held the railroad owed her no duty, because harm to her was not foreseeable. Judge William Andrews, dissenting, said the question was proximate cause, a matter of fairness and policy. PSU-2.2 develops the doctrine.

sections.title: Two Fires
sections.body_md: You know the but-for test. It fails when two causes are each enough. Two separate fires, each set carelessly, merge and burn a house. Without either fire the house still burns, so neither passes but-for. Yet both are clearly causes. Richard Wright, building on Hart and Honoré, proposed the NESS test: a cause is a Necessary Element of a Sufficient Set of conditions. Each fire is necessary to one sufficient set, so each counts.

sections.title: Proximate Cause as Policy
sections.body_md: Legal realists argued that proximate cause is not about cause at all. Leon Green said courts use causal language to hide choices about how far liability should reach. Andrews's Palsgraf dissent admitted as much, calling it practical politics. On this view, a lawyer arguing proximate cause should argue fairness, risk and policy openly, because that is what really decides the case.
sections.example: A careless driver damages a power line, and a factory miles away loses a day of production. Courts often deny the factory recovery. Realists say the real reason is fear of endless liability, not a missing cause.

sections.title: Moral Luck
sections.body_md: You know law blames those who cause harm. Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel, in essays of 1976, named a puzzle called moral luck. Two drivers are equally careless. One hits a child who runs into the road, the other hits no one. Their choices were identical, yet law and ordinary judgment blame the first far more. If blame should track only what we control, outcome-based liability looks unfair.
sections.example: Two nurses each misread a dose chart in the same way on the same night. One patient is fine because the pharmacy caught the error. The other is harmed. Should only one nurse be sued?

One patient is fine because the pharmacy caught the error. The other is harmed. Should only one nurse be sued?

sections.title: Outcome Responsibility
sections.body_md: Honoré answered in his 1988 essay Responsibility and Luck. He argued that we are responsible for the outcomes of our actions, good and bad, as a condition of being agents at all. We take credit for our lucky successes, so we must own our unlucky harms. Outcome responsibility explains why law cares about results, while fault explains how much. Critics reply that it makes the poor and unlucky carry costs they could not avoid.
sections.example: A chef whose new dish wins an award proudly claims the credit. If the same dish makes a diner sick through a mistake in her kitchen, Honoré says she cannot disown that result.

sections.title: No Right Without a Remedy
sections.body_md: A remedy is what the law does for you when your right is broken. An old maxim says ubi jus ibi remedium: where there is a right, there is a remedy. In Ashby v. White (1703), an English voter wrongly refused a vote sued the officials. Chief Justice Holt, in a dissent the House of Lords later upheld, said a right means nothing if there is no way to vindicate it, and the voter could recover damages even without proving money loss.
sections.example: A city clerk refuses to register a citizen to vote, though she is eligible. Her right is plain. Unless some court can order registration or award damages, the right protects her no more than a wish.

sections.title: Kinds of Remedy
sections.body_md: Courts offer a few basic remedies. Damages are money to make up for a loss. An injunction is an order to do or stop doing something. Specific performance orders a party to keep a contract. Restitution makes someone give back a gain they should not keep. A declaration states the parties' rights. Choosing the right remedy is often what matters most to a client.
sections.example: A tenant's landlord shuts off her heat in winter. Money next year will not keep her children warm tonight. Her lawyer asks for an injunction ordering the heat turned back on.

sections.title: Corrective Justice
sections.body_md: You learned that remedies make rights real. Aristotle, in Book V of the Nicomachean Ethics, explained why. Corrective justice restores a balance between two people that a wrong upset. If I take your money, the remedy gives it back, no matter who is richer. The court looks only at the wrong between the parties, not at their wealth or virtue. This is why a poor thief must still repay a rich victim.
sections.example: A billionaire's careless driver dents a student's old car. The student gets the repair cost, not more because the driver is rich and not less because the car is cheap. The remedy restores exactly what the wrong took.

sections.title: Distributive Justice
sections.body_md: Distributive justice asks a different question: how should a society share benefits and burdens among all its members? Taxes, welfare and public schools are distributive. Aristotle saw that the two kinds of justice follow different logic. Corrective justice uses strict equality between the two parties. Distributive justice uses some criterion, such as need or merit, across the whole community. Mixing them causes confusion in remedy disputes.
sections.example: A judge feels sorry for a struggling defendant and cuts the damages owed to a wealthy plaintiff. That uses distributive reasoning inside a corrective case. Most private law theorists say the judge erred.

sections.title: Weinrib's Private Law
sections.body_md: Ernest Weinrib, in The Idea of Private Law (1995), argued that private law is corrective justice through and through. The defendant's duty and the plaintiff's right are two sides of one relation, and the remedy undoes the wrong within that relation. On this view, goals like deterring accidents or spreading losses are foreign to private law. Jules Coleman offered a mixed view that kept corrective justice central while allowing other goals.

sections.title: Property Rules and Liability Rules
sections.body_md: You know corrective justice says a remedy undoes the wrong. Guido Calabresi and A. Douglas Melamed, in a 1972 article known as One View of the Cathedral, showed that law can protect the same right in different ways. A property rule protects it by injunction: no one may take it without your consent. A liability rule lets others take it if they pay damages set by a court. An inalienability rule forbids transfer altogether, as with organs or votes.
sections.example: A factory's smoke harms a neighbor's home. A property rule shuts the factory unless the neighbor agrees to a price. A liability rule lets it keep running if it pays court-set damages. Same right, different protection.

sections.title: Civil Recourse
sections.body_md: John Goldberg and Benjamin Zipursky challenged both corrective justice and economics with civil recourse theory. They argue tort law gives wronged people a power to act against those who wronged them, through the state's courts, in place of private revenge. The victim decides whether to sue. This explains why a plaintiff can drop a case, and why remedies belong to the person wronged rather than to society.
sections.example: A woman defamed by a coworker may choose to sue, settle or let it go. No prosecutor decides for her. Civil recourse theory says that choice is the point: the law hands her a lawful way to answer the wrong.

sections.title: Remedies Shape Rights

If a court shrinks the remedy, it shrinks the right, even if the words of the right stay the same.

sections.title: The Access Gap
sections.body_md: You know a right is only as strong as its remedy. A remedy is only as strong as a person's ability to reach it. Many people with valid claims never file, because lawyers cost money, courts are slow and forms are confusing. A theory of remedies that ignores this gap describes a system that works mostly for the well-resourced. Any account of what remedies should be must ask who can actually use them. This is part of ProSeU's own purpose.
sections.example: A worker is owed 900 dollars in unpaid wages. A lawyer would cost more than that. Without small claims courts, fee-shifting rules or legal aid, her right exists only on paper.

red.summary: Learn the difference between power and legitimacy. Legitimacy is the right to rule, and it explains why people accept law even when no one forces them.

sections.title: Power Versus Legitimacy
sections.body_md: Power is the ability to make people do things. Legitimacy is the right to do so, as judged by those subject to it or by sound reasons. A gang can have power over a neighborhood without legitimacy. A court with no army has little raw power, yet people follow its rulings because they see them as legitimate. Law depends on legitimacy far more than on force, because no state can watch everyone all the time.

sections.title: Weber's Three Types
sections.body_md: Max Weber, the German sociologist, described three kinds of legitimate authority in Economy and Society. Traditional authority rests on custom, as with a hereditary chief. Charismatic authority rests on a leader's personal gifts and followers' devotion. Legal-rational authority rests on rules made by proper procedures, and officials who hold offices rather than personal power. Modern legal systems claim legal-rational authority. Weber described how people view authority. He did not say any type was justified.
sections.example: A village elder settles a land dispute because elders always have. A movement follows its founder because she inspires them. A city clerk issues a permit because the zoning code says so. Three different sources of the same willingness to obey.

sections.title: Why Legitimacy Matters
sections.body_md: When people see law as legitimate, they obey voluntarily, cooperate with police and courts, and accept losing. When they do not, the law must rely on force, which is costly and breeds resentment. For lawyers, legitimacy is practical, not abstract: clients trust a process they see as fair, and courts carefully guard their own legitimacy whenever they decide hard cases.
sections.example: After a fair trial, a landlord who loses an eviction case usually complies with the judgment without a single officer appearing. He accepts the result because he accepts the court's right to decide.

sections.title: King Rex's Eight Failures
sections.body_md: You learned that law depends on legitimacy. Lon Fuller, in The Morality of Law (1964), told the story of King Rex, who tried to rule and failed eight ways. He made no general rules and decided case by case. He kept rules secret. He made them retroactive. He wrote them so they could not be understood. He made them contradict each other. He demanded the impossible. He changed them constantly. And his officials ignored the rules he published.
sections.example: Rex is a fable, but each failure is real. Secret police orders, laws in a language citizens cannot read, and officials who ignore published rules all appear in history. Each leaves people unable to plan their lives.

He demanded the impossible. He changed them constantly. And his officials ignored the rules he published. Example: Rex is a fable, but each failure is real. sections.title: The Inner Morality of Law
sections.body_md: From Rex's failures, Fuller drew eight principles of legality: rules must be general, public, prospective, clear, consistent, possible to obey, stable over time, and matched by official action. He called these the inner morality of law. A system that totally fails one, he said, is not merely bad law but not a legal system at all. These principles respect people as agents who can plan their lives by known rules.
sections.example: A city posts a new parking rule today and fines everyone who parked there last week. That breaks prospectivity. Drivers could not obey a rule that did not yet exist.

That breaks prospectivity. Drivers could not obey a rule that did not yet exist.

sections.title: The Rule of Law
sections.body_md: The rule of law means government under known, general rules that bind officials as well as citizens, applied by independent courts. Fuller's principles are its formal core. A lawyer who spots a secret rule, a retroactive penalty or an official ignoring the rules has found a rule of law argument.

sections.title: Radbruch's Formula
sections.body_md: Gustav Radbruch, a German legal philosopher, argued in 1946 that statutes normally bind even when unjust. But where a statute's conflict with justice reaches an intolerable degree, it must yield as false law. Where a statute does not even aim at justice, for example by deliberately denying equality, it is not law at all. German courts later applied the formula to East German border guards who shot people fleeing to the West.
sections.example: A guard who shot a man climbing the Berlin Wall pointed to East German border law that he said allowed it. German courts held that a rule permitting the killing of unarmed people simply for leaving was so unjust it could not shield him.

sections.title: Critical Theories
sections.body_md: Critics argue that legitimacy can hide power. Marxist theory sees law as serving the dominant class. Critical legal studies, associated with Duncan Kennedy and Roberto Unger, argued that doctrine is indeterminate and that legal reasoning dresses political choices as neutral. Feminist theorists such as Catharine MacKinnon argued law takes a male point of view as neutral. Critical race theory, from Derrick Bell and Kimberlé Crenshaw, examined how law can entrench racial hierarchy even when it speaks of equality.
sections.example: A rule that bans everyone, rich or poor, from sleeping under bridges sounds neutral. The French writer Anatole France mocked such equality. Critical theorists ask who actually bears the burden of a rule that looks neutral on its face.

sections.title: Democratic Justification
sections.body_md: You know critics say legitimacy can mask power. Jürgen Habermas, in Between Facts and Norms (1992), answered that law is legitimate when those subject to it could agree to it as participants in rational public discussion. Law gets its authority from a fair democratic process in which citizens are authors as well as addressees of law. Critics ask whether real politics ever meets this ideal, and what follows when it does not.

sections.title: Fair Procedure
sections.body_md: Tom Tyler's research, reported in Why People Obey the Law (1990), found that people obey law mainly when they see the process as fair, not mainly because of fear of punishment or favorable outcomes. Being heard, treated with respect and judged neutrally matter most. This suggests legitimacy is earned in every courtroom and every police stop. For lawyers, it means procedure is not a formality. It is how law earns the right to be obeyed.

Thompson, a Marxist historian, surprised readers of Whigs and Hunters (1975) by calling the rule of law an unqualified human good, because it restrains the powerful too.
